Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space of dimension $n$, let $B$ be a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form, and put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. A vector $u$ is **anisotropic** when $Q(u)\ne0$; a subspace $U$ is **totally isotropic** when $B|_{U\times U}=0$. Define $O(V,B)=\{A\in\operatorname{GL}(V):B(Av,Aw)=B(v,w)\}$ and $SO(V,B)=\{A\in O(V,B):\det A=1\}$. For $U\le V$, put $U^\perp=\{v:B(v,U)=0\}$. Then:

1. $\dim U^\perp=n-\dim U$, and every totally isotropic $U$ has $\dim U\le n/2$.
2. Every such $(V,B)$ has a basis of pairwise orthogonal anisotropic vectors.
3. For $A\in O(V,B)$, $\operatorname{im}(A-I)=\ker(A-I)^\perp$.
4. For anisotropic $u$, the map $r_u(v)=v-2B(v,u)u/Q(u)$ is an orthogonal reflection: it fixes $u^\perp$, sends $u$ to $-u$, and has determinant $-1$.

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, $O(V,B)=\{I\}$ and the empty product proves the claim. If $n=1$, choose an anisotropic basis vector $u$ by [F1]. Every $A\in O(V,B)$ sends $u$ to $\pm u$, so $A=I$ or $A=r_u$; these have reflection lengths zero and one, respectively, and the parity agrees with the determinant. We now prove the induction step for $n\ge2$.

Suppose $n\ge2$ and inductively assume the theorem in smaller dimensions. If $K$ contains an anisotropic $u$, then $A$ fixes $u$ and preserves the nondegenerate space $u^\perp$. The induction hypothesis factors $A|_{u^\perp}$ into at most $n-1$ reflections with normals in $u^\perp$; extending these reflections by the identity on $\mathbb Ru$ gives the same reflections in $V$ and their product equals $A$.

Suppose instead $W$ is not totally isotropic. Then $w\mapsto Q(w)$ and $w\mapsto Q((A-I)w)$ are nonzero real polynomials: the first by nondegeneracy and the second because some vector in $W$ is anisotropic. Their product is a nonzero polynomial because the real polynomial ring is an integral domain. A nonzero polynomial on $\mathbb R^n$ does not vanish everywhere: for $n=1$ it has finitely many roots; for $n>1$, write $P(x,t)=\sum_j p_j(x)t^j$ with a nonzero coefficient $p_j$, use induction to choose $x$ with $p_j(x)\ne0$, and then choose $t$ outside the finite root set of the nonzero one-variable polynomial $P(x,t)$. Choose $w$ where the product is nonzero and put $u=(A-I)w$. Then both $w$ and $u$ are anisotropic.

It remains that both $K$ and $W$ are totally isotropic. By [F1], $W=K^\perp$. Since $K$ and $W$ are both totally isotropic, [F1] gives $\dim K\le n/2$ and $\dim W\le n/2$. But $\dim W=n-\dim K$, so both dimensions equal $n/2$; the inclusion $K\subseteq K^\perp=W$ then gives $K=W=K^\perp$ and $n=2\dim K$. The map $A$ is the identity on $K$, and because $(A-I)V=W=K$ it is also the identity on $V/K$. In a basis extending a basis of $K$, its matrix is block triangular with identity diagonal blocks, so $\det A=1$.

Symmetry and orthogonality give $B((A+I)w,u)=B(Aw,Aw)-B(Aw,w)+B(w,Aw)-B(w,w)=0$. Thus $(A+I)w$ is fixed by $r_u$ and $u=(A-I)w$ is negated, so $r_uAw=w$. The orthogonal map $r_uA$ has the anisotropic fixed vector $w$, and the argument of step 1.2 factors it with at most $n-1$ reflections. Prepending $r_u$ factors $A$ with at most $n$.

Since $n$ is even in step 1.4, choose anisotropic $u$ and put $A_1=r_uA$. Then $\det A_1=-1$, so $A_1$ cannot be in the isotropic case of step 1.4. Steps 1.2 and 2.1 give a factorization of $A_1$ of length at most $n$. Each reflection has determinant $-1$, so this length is odd; because $n$ is even it is at most $n-1$. The identity $A=r_uA_1$ now gives at most $n$ reflections.

Every reflection has determinant $-1$, hence any reflection factorization of $A$ has parity determined by $\det A$. The constructed length is at most $n$ in all cases, and its parity is even precisely for determinant $1$. This proves the assertion, including the isotropic kernel and moved-space case.

For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.

derivations.claim: On the tensor algebra, send a word $v_1\cdots v_m$ to $(-1)^m v_1\cdots v_m$ for $\alpha$, and to $v_m\cdots v_1$ for $t$. The first is an algebra automorphism and the second reverses products. Each defining relation $v^2-Q(v)1$ is fixed by both maps. The ideal generated by these relations is therefore invariant under each map: applying either map to a generator of the ideal gives another generator, with left and right factors exchanged for $t$. Thus both maps descend to the quotient and square to the identity.
Their composite $\bar x=t(\alpha(x))$ is an order-reversing involution and satisfies $\bar u=-u$ for $u\in V$. Hence $N(u)=u\bar u=-u^2=-Q(u)1$.

For $k=0$, the empty product is $1$ and $N(1)=1$. If $N(y)$ is scalar, then $N(xy)=xy\overline{xy}=xy\bar y\bar x=xN(y)\bar x=N(y)N(x)$. Induction on $k\ge1$, starting with step 2.1, therefore gives $N(u_1\cdots u_k)=\prod_{j=1}^k(-Q(u_j))1$.

Let $x\in\Gamma$ and $y_v=\rho_x(v)\in V$. Since $\alpha(y_v)=-y_v$, applying $\alpha$ to $y_v=\alpha(x)vx^{-1}$ gives $xv\alpha(x)^{-1}=\alpha(x)vx^{-1}$, that is, $\rho_{\alpha(x)}(v)=\rho_x(v)$. Using this equality in one factor and [F1] gives $2B(y_v,y_w)1=y_vy_w+y_wy_v=\alpha(x)(vw+wv)\alpha(x)^{-1}=2B(v,w)1$. Thus $\rho_x$ preserves $B$; it is injective because multiplication by invertible elements is injective, and finite dimensionality makes its image all of $V$.

If $n=0$, [F2] gives $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=\mathbb R$, so every kernel element is scalar. If $n>0$ and $\rho_x$ is the identity, then $\alpha(x)e_i=e_i x$ for every vector of an orthogonal anisotropic basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$. Write $x=x_0+x_1$ with even and odd parts. For a square-free monomial $e_I$ of length $r$, moving $e_i$ past it gives commutation sign $(-1)^r$ when $i\notin I$ and $(-1)^{r-1}$ when $i\in I$. For each nonempty even $I$, choose $i\in I$: the required commutation fails; for each odd $I$, choose $i\in I$: the required anticommutation fails. Let $(V,B)$ be a finite-dimensional nondegenerate real quadratic space, $Q(v)=B(v,v)$, and let $\Gamma$ and $\rho_x(v)=\alpha(x)vx^{-1}$ be as in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]]. For anisotropic $u$, $\rho_u=r_u$. Every $x\in\Gamma$ acts by an element of $O(V,B)$, is homogeneous, and is a nonzero scalar times a product of anisotropic vectors. The kernel of $x\mapsto\rho_x$ on $\Gamma$ is exactly $\mathbb R^\times 1$; consequently the unrestricted normalizer in the definition is a group and agrees with its homogeneous part.

Let $\Gamma$, Pin, $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}$, $N(x)=x\bar x$, and $\rho$ have the definitions in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]] and [[lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm]]. Then $N$ is scalar-valued and multiplicative on $\Gamma$. For $x=u_1\cdots u_k$ with anisotropic $u_j$,

$$N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k(-Q(u_j)).$$

The subgroup generated by $|Q(u)|=1$ vectors is exactly $\{x\in\Gamma:N(x)\in\{1,-1\}\}$; it consists of normalized anisotropic-vector products, with scalar $-1$ included when $V=0$. derivations.claim: Let $A\in O(V,B)$. By [F1], write $A=r_{u_1}\cdots r_{u_k}$. Replacing each anisotropic $u_j$ by $u_j/\sqrt{|Q(u_j)|}$ preserves its reflection and gives a Pin generator; [F2] shows their product maps to $A$. Thus $\rho$ maps Pin onto $O(V,B)$.

Each normalized vector has determinant $-1$ under $\rho$. Therefore an even product maps into $SO(V,B)$, and every $A\in SO(V,B)$ has an even reflection factorization by [F1]; its normalized lift lies in full Spin. Hence $\rho$ maps full Spin onto $SO(V,B)$.

The kernel of either restriction is contained in the scalar kernel $\mathbb R^\times$ by [F2]. If a scalar $\lambda$ lies in Pin, [F3] gives $N(\lambda)=\lambda^2\in\{1,-1\}$. Since $\lambda$ is real, $\lambda^2>0$, so $\lambda^2=1$ and $\lambda=\pm1$. Conversely both scalars belong to Pin and full Spin and act trivially. This proves exactness with kernel $\{1,-1\}$.

Scalars are central in the Clifford algebra, so the two kernels are central. For a definite form with $n>0$, the normalized-vector set $U=\{u:|Q(u)|=1\}$ is a compact sphere. Given $x\in\operatorname{Pin}$, factor $\rho_x$ by [F1] into at most $n$ reflections and lift them to a normalized-vector product $y$. Then $xy^{-1}$ is scalar by [F2], and step 1.3 makes it $\pm1$; hence every Pin element is $\pm$ a product of at most $n$ vectors. If $x$ is full-even Spin, its image has determinant $1$, so [F1] gives an even reflection factorization and the same argument gives an even product of at most $n$ vectors. Each fixed-length product is the continuous image of a finite product of $U$, hence compact; the groups are finite unions of these images. In dimension zero both are the finite group $\{1,-1\}$.

For $n>0$, choose a submultiplicative matrix norm and shrink a neighborhood $U$ of $I$ in $SO(V,B)$ until $\|A-I\|$, $\|A^T-I\|$, and $\|A^{-1}-I\|$ are all less than $1$. Then the series $L=\log A=\sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^{m+1}(A-I)^m/m$ and the corresponding series for $A^T$ and $A^{-1}$ converge absolutely and continuously. The scalar power-series identities, by absolute Cauchy products, give $\exp L=A$, $\log(A^T)=L^T$, and $\log(A^{-1})=-L$. From $A^TJA=J$ one gets $JAJ=A^{-T}$, so conjugating the logarithm series gives $JLJ=-L^T$, equivalently $L^TJ+JL=0$.

For $i<j$, direct use of [F1] gives $[e_ie_j,e_k]=2(B(e_j,e_k)e_i-B(e_i,e_k)e_j)$. The $n(n-1)/2$ bivectors therefore map under $b\mapsto\operatorname{ad}_b|_V$ to a basis of the matrices $L$ satisfying $L^TJ+JL=0$: each coefficient $c_{ij}$ independently gives entries $L_{ij}=2c_{ij}\epsilon_j$ and $L_{ji}=-2c_{ij}\epsilon_i$. Thus there is a unique bivector $b(L)=\sum_{i<j}c_{ij}e_ie_j$ with $[b(L),v]=Lv$ for every $v\in V$, and it depends linearly and continuously on $L$.

Set $s(A)=\exp(b(L))$ in the finite-dimensional Clifford algebra. Since $b(L)$ is even, $\alpha(s(A))=s(A)$. The convergent commutator series gives $s(A)v s(A)^{-1}=\exp(\operatorname{ad}_{b(L)})(v)=\exp(L)v=Av$, so $s(A)\in\Gamma$ and $\rho(s(A))=A$.

Reversion negates each bivector, hence Clifford conjugation sends $b(L)$ to $-b(L)$ and $\overline{\exp(b(L))}=\exp(-b(L))$. Therefore $N(s(A))=\exp(b(L))\exp(-b(L))=1$. By [F4], $s(A)\in\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}$. Continuity of matrix logarithm on $U$, of $b(L)$, and of the finite-dimensional algebra exponential proves continuity of $s$, with $s(I)=1$.

$$
\mathrm{Cl}_{p,q}^0\cong \mathrm{Cl}_{q,p-1};
$$

if $p=0$ and $q>0$, then $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q}^0\cong\mathrm{Cl}_{0,q-1}$. derivations.claim: Choose a pairwise orthogonal anisotropic basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$ by [F1], and put $u_i=e_i/\sqrt{|Q(e_i)|}$, so each $u_i$ is normalized. By PBW in this ordered basis, every even basis monomial $e_{i_1}\cdots e_{i_{2k}}$ is a nonzero real scalar multiple of the even normalized-vector product $u_{i_1}\cdots u_{i_{2k}}$. That product belongs to full-even Spin, so the real span of full-even Spin contains a basis of $\mathrm{Cl}^0$. Conversely every full-even Spin element belongs to $\mathrm{Cl}^0$. Therefore $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}})=\mathrm{Cl}^0$. A real subspace is Spin-invariant exactly when it is invariant under this linear span, so a given $\mathrm{Cl}^0$-module and its Spin restriction have the same invariant subspaces and commutants. Moreover any Spin intertwiner between two such restrictions intertwines the spanning algebra; hence their module-isomorphism and Spin-isomorphism classes agree, and an extending algebra action is uniquely determined.

For a division algebra $D$ and $r\ge1$, the standard column module $D^r$ is simple over $M_r(D)$: from any nonzero column, matrix units move a nonzero coordinate to any position and left multiplication by $D$ produces arbitrary coordinates. Conversely, if $M$ is a finite-dimensional simple left $M_r(D)$-module, some diagonal matrix unit $E_{ii}$ acts nontrivially; matrix units transfer a nonzero vector to $E_{11}M$. This is a left $D$-module. If it had dimension greater than one, choose a proper nonzero left $D$-subspace $W\subset E_{11}M$ and form $N=\sum_{i=1}^r E_{i1}W$. Matrix multiplication shows $N$ is an $M_r(D)$-submodule, and $E_{11}N=W$; hence $N$ is nonzero and proper, contradicting simplicity of $M$. Thus $E_{11}M\cong D$, and $D^r\to M$, $(d_i)\mapsto\sum_i E_{i1}(d_i)v$, is a nonzero module map; simplicity of $D^r$ makes it an isomorphism.

An endomorphism of $D^r$ commuting with $M_r(D)$ must commute with every $E_{ij}$ and every diagonal scalar matrix; it is therefore the same right multiplication by some $d\in D$ in every coordinate. The commutant is $D^{\mathrm{op}}$. For a product of matrix algebras, the central identity idempotents split every module; in a simple module exactly one factor acts nontrivially, so each factor gives one simple type and distinct factors give inequivalent modules.

Applying [L1] to identify the even algebra and [A1] to classify its real matrix factors, the matrix-algebra result of steps 1.2–2.1 gives exactly the column modules, dimensions, and commutant types stated. By step 1.1 these are exactly the irreducible Clifford spinor restrictions to full-even Spin. This calculation does not identify the type of a full Clifford module without computing its even-subalgebra factors.

In dimensions $0$ and $1$, the even monomials are just scalars, so $\mathrm{Cl}^0\cong\mathbb R$. In dimension $2$, put $E=e_1e_2$ for an orthogonal basis normalized so that $Q(e_i)=\pm1$. Such normalization is obtained by dividing each anisotropic basis vector by $\sqrt{|Q(e_i)|}$. Then $E^2=-Q(e_1)Q(e_2)$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^0=\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R E$. If the signature is definite, $E^2=-1$ and this is $\mathbb C$; its standard real module has dimension $2$ and commutant $\mathbb C$. If the signature is $(1,1)$, $E^2=1$ and $\mathbb R[E]/(E^2-1)\cong\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R$ via $a+bE\mapsto(a+b,a-b)$, giving two one-dimensional real modules. Step 1.1 transfers these classifications to Spin.

derivations.claim: The maps are continuous because the twisted action uses only finite-dimensional algebra multiplication, the grading involution, and inversion on the open set of invertible elements. By [F2], shrink a neighborhood $U$ of the identity in $SO(V,B)$ until the section is defined on $U$. For every $A\in U$, [F1] says the fiber is exactly $\{s(A),-s(A)\}$.

Since the finite-dimensional Clifford algebra is Hausdorff and $1\ne-1$, choose an open neighborhood $W$ of $1$ disjoint from $-W$. Since $s(I)=1$, shrink $U$ so $s(U)\subset W$ and $-s(U)\subset -W$. Then $\rho^{-1}(U)\cap W=s(U)$ and $\rho^{-1}(U)\cap(-W)=-s(U)$ are disjoint open subsets of $\rho^{-1}(U)$; each maps homeomorphically to $U$, with inverse $s$ or $-s$. Thus the map on full-even Spin is a two-sheeted covering near the identity.

If $n=0$, then [F5] gives $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=\mathbb R$, all its elements are even, and the definition gives $\operatorname{Pin}(0)=\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(0)=\{1,-1\}$. The target groups $O(0)$ and $SO(0)$ are both the singleton $\{I_0\}$, and both action maps are the two-to-one map from the discrete two-point group to a point. Thus both maps are covering maps in dimension zero. Now suppose $n>0$. This is a topological assertion in addition to the algebraic exactness of those sequences.

Let $p,q>0$ and use signature $(+^p,-^q)$. In the polar decomposition of $A\in SO(p,q)$ from [[lem-real-orthogonal-polar-decomposition]], write $K=K_+\oplus K_-$ with $K_+\in O(p)$ and $K_-\in O(q)$. Then $\det K_+=\det K_-\in\{1,-1\}$, and

$$SO_0(p,q)=\{A\in SO(p,q):\det K_+=1\}=\rho(\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}(p,q)).$$

For definite signature, $SO(p,q)$ is connected and every full-even Spin element has norm $1$, so full-even Spin and norm-one Spin have the same image and are the same subgroup. In signature $(1,1)$, the norm-one preimage of $SO_0(1,1)$ has two connected components; it is not the identity component of full-even Spin.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $V=\mathbb R^n$ have its positive-definite inner product. Give $S^{n-1}=\{v:Q(v)=1\}$ the subspace topology and let

$$p:\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n)\to S^{n-1},\qquad p(x)=\rho_x(e_n).$$

Then $p$ is onto, the stabilizer of $e_n$ is the embedded $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n-1)$ generated by even products from $e_n^\perp$, and $p$ is a locally trivial right $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}(n-1)$ bundle. For unit $a$ and unit $v$ with $B(v,a)>-1$, the explicit local section is

$$s_a(v)=\frac{1+va}{\sqrt{2(1+B(v,a))}}.$$

The bundle admits a finite partition of unity whose functions have closed supports contained in the corresponding local chart domains.

Assume AC. Every numerable fiber bundle, with its supplied ordinary local product charts and support-subordinate locally finite partition of unity, is a Hurewicz fibration in all ordinary spaces. In particular a bundle of CGWH spaces with these charts is a Hurewicz fibration in CGWH. AC is used to well-order the set of finite chart words. No selection of a chart for every base point or of a separate lift for every path is made.

For a based Serre fibration $p:(E,e_0)\to(B,b_0)$ with fiber $F=p^{-1}(b_0)$, the sequence
$$\cdots\to\pi_n(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_n(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_n(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_{n-1}(F)\to\cdots\to\pi_1(B)\xrightarrow{\partial_p}\pi_0(F)\xrightarrow{i_*}\pi_0(E)\xrightarrow{p_*}\pi_0(B)$$
is exact wherever there is an incoming and outgoing arrow. Basepoints are $e_0,b_0$ as appropriate. Exactness means incoming image equals the inverse image of the distinguished element. Arrows are homomorphisms where both group structures are defined; the component terms are pointed sets. The last arrow is onto precisely when $p(E)$ meets every path component of $B$.

There is a right action of $\pi_1(B,b_0)$ on $\pi_0(F)$: $[e]\cdot[\gamma]$ is the endpoint component of a lift of $\gamma$ starting at $e$, with loop products traversed left-to-right. Its orbits are precisely the fibers of $i_*:\pi_0(F)\to\pi_0(E)$, and the stabilizer of $[e_0]$ is $p_*\pi_1(E,e_0)$. Our boundary convention gives $\partial_p[\gamma]=[e_0]\cdot[\gamma]^{-1}$. These assertions require no AC.
For every natural number $n\ge2$, the unit sphere $S^n\subseteq\mathbb R^{n+1}$ is simply connected ([[def-simply-connected]]).

Let $\Gamma$, Pin, $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}$, $N(x)=x\bar x$, and $\rho$ have the definitions in [[def-real-clifford-group-and-normalized-pin-spin]] and [[lem-real-clifford-involutions-and-norm]]. Then $N$ is scalar-valued and multiplicative on $\Gamma$. For $x=u_1\cdots u_k$ with anisotropic $u_j$,

$$N(x)=\prod_{j=1}^k(-Q(u_j)).$$

The subgroup generated by $|Q(u)|=1$ vectors is exactly $\{x\in\Gamma:N(x)\in\{1,-1\}\}$; it consists of normalized anisotropic-vector products, with scalar $-1$ included when $V=0$. Its even part consists of the even products and is $\operatorname{Spin}_{\mathrm{full}}$; $\operatorname{Spin}_{N=1}$ is the norm-one subgroup of this full even group.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic not $2$, let $V$ be finite-dimensional of dimension $n$, and let $B$ be any symmetric bilinear form on $V$, possibly degenerate; put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Fix an ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$. Then

$$1,\qquad \bar e_{i_1}\cdots\bar e_{i_r}\quad(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n)$$

is a $k$-basis of $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$, so $\dim_k\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=2^n$. Give $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ the word-length filtration $F_{-1}=0$ and, for $m\ge0$, let $F_m$ be the span of products of at most $m$ canonical generators. The natural graded algebra map

$$\Lambda V\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}_F\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=\bigoplus_{m\ge0}F_m/F_{m-1}$$

that sends $v\in V$ to the degree-one class of $\bar v$ is an isomorphism, where the graded product is induced by $F_pF_q\subseteq F_{p+q}$. No nondegeneracy hypothesis is needed.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

For every $n\ge2$, $\operatorname{Spin}(n)$ is path connected. By [F6], each element is a product of an even number of unit vectors, possibly multiplied by $-1$. The unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ is path connected: non-antipodal points join by a great-circle arc, and antipodal points join by two such arcs through a third point. For each pair of unit factors choose paths from a fixed unit vector $e_1$ to the two factors and multiply the two paths; at the initial endpoint their product is $e_1^2=1$. Concatenating these paths joins $1$ to the product. The remaining scalar $-1$ joins to $1$ along $t\mapsto\cos(\pi t)+e_1e_2\sin(\pi t)$. It lies in full-even Spin because
\[
\cos(\pi t)+e_1e_2\sin(\pi t)=e_1\bigl(\cos(\pi t)e_1+\sin(\pi t)e_2\bigr),
\]
and both factors are unit vectors; the path starts at $1$ and ends at $-1$.

In dimension $3$, [F7] gives basis $1,e_1e_2,e_2e_3,e_3e_1$ for $\mathrm{Cl}^0_{3,0}$. Direct multiplication gives the quaternion relations, Clifford conjugation negates each bivector, and hence $N(a+b_1e_1e_2+b_2e_2e_3+b_3e_3e_1)=a^2+b_1^2+b_2^2+b_3^2$. A bivector $b=b_1e_2e_3+b_2e_3e_1+b_3e_1e_2$ corresponds to the vector $b_1e_1+b_2e_2+b_3e_3$ under the three-dimensional Hodge star; choosing an oriented orthonormal basis in its perpendicular plane gives $b=\beta uw$ with $u,w$ orthonormal and $\beta=\sqrt{b_1^2+b_2^2+b_3^2}$. If $a^2+\beta^2=1$, the vector $v=au+\beta w$ is unit and $uv=a+b$. For $b=0$, the elements $\pm1$ are the empty product and a product $u(-u)$. Thus every unit quaternion is in Spin, and every Spin element has norm one, so $\operatorname{Spin}(3)=S^3$. By [F5], this group is simply connected.

For $n\ge4$, the sphere bundle in [F2] has a finite subordinate partition of unity, so it is numerable; [F3] and [A1] make it a Hurewicz, hence Serre, fibration. Its fiber is $\operatorname{Spin}(n-1)$ and its base is $S^{n-1}$. By the induction hypothesis the fiber is simply connected, and [F5] makes the base simply connected. The exact segment $\pi_1(\operatorname{Spin}(n-1))\to\pi_1(\operatorname{Spin}(n))\to\pi_1(S^{n-1})$ from [F4] therefore forces $\pi_1(\operatorname{Spin}(n))=0$. Step 1.1 gives path connectedness, so Spin$(n)$ is simply connected for all $n\ge3$.

By [F1], Spin$(n)\to SO(n)$ is a connected covering with connected simply connected total space. By definition this is the universal covering space; since the map is a group homomorphism, it is the universal covering group. The induction begins at $n=3$ in step 2.1 and proceeds by step 3.1, with the exact choice use recorded in [A1].

In $\mathrm{Cl}_{0,1}$, $f^2=-1$ and Pin is $\{1,-1,f,-f\}\cong C_4$; its reflection lift has square $-1$. In both cases the even subgroup is $\{1,-1\}$.

In $\mathrm{Cl}_{2,0}$ put $E=e_1e_2$. Then $E^2=-1$, and by [F3] the even algebra is exactly $\mathbb R\oplus\mathbb R E\cong\mathbb C$. For $a^2+b^2=1$, $a+bE$ is a product of two unit vectors: $e_1(ae_1+be_2)=a+bE$. Thus every unit $a+bE$ belongs to Spin, and conversely every even unit product has norm one, so Spin$(2)=\{a+bE:a^2+b^2=1\}$.

For $\theta\in\mathbb R$, let $g_\theta=\cos(\theta/2)-E\sin(\theta/2)$. Since $g_\theta^{-1}=\cos(\theta/2)+E\sin(\theta/2)$, direct multiplication using $Ee_1=-e_2$ and $e_1E=e_2$ gives $\rho_{g_\theta}(e_1)=\cos\theta\,e_1+\sin\theta\,e_2$ and $\rho_{g_\theta}(e_2)=-\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2$. Therefore the angle doubles; $g_{2\pi}=-1$ and $g_{4\pi}=1$.

The matrices in the Example satisfy $A^2=B^2=I$ and $AB=-BA=\operatorname{diag}(-i,i)$. Hence $(z_1A+z_2B)^2=(z_1^2+z_2^2)I$ for all $z_1,z_2\in\mathbb C$. Applying [F4] to the complexification of the positive plane defines a unital complex Clifford action on $S$. Its image contains $P_+=(I+iAB)/2=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ and $P_-=(I-iAB)/2=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$, as well as $P_+A$ and $P_-A$, which are the other two matrix units. The image is therefore all of $M_2(\mathbb C)$; [F3] gives complex dimension $4$ for the source, so this map is an algebra isomorphism. Every nonzero invariant subspace contains both coordinate vectors by applying these matrix units to a nonzero vector, proving irreducibility of the complex dimension-$2$ Clifford module.

Since $c(E)=AB=\operatorname{diag}(-i,i)$, the operator $c(\omega)=iAB$ has the displayed eigenspaces $S^\pm$, each a complex line. Restricting the Clifford action to the circle in step 1.2 gives on these lines the scalars $a-ib$ and $a+ib$, of absolute value one. The scalar functions are continuous in $(a,b)$, and multiplicativity of the Clifford action makes them group characters; the one-dimensional modules are irreducible.
